conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m Sarah, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad you’re here—taking this step shows real strength.

Today I’ll be asking you the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, evidence-based screen for the kinds of mood changes many new mothers notice in the first weeks and months after birth. We use it to be sure we’re not missing anything that could help you feel better.

I want you to know this conversation is confidential and judgment-free. There are no “wrong” answers; whatever you’re feeling is worth talking about. We’ll go through ten short questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days, and I’ll re-phrase them in everyday language so they’re easy to answer. If anything feels too difficult, we can pause.

Ready to begin?

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has that felt easy, sometimes hard, very hard, or not possible at all?

It’s been pretty hard lately. I can still laugh if something’s really funny, but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to—maybe once or twice this week I’ve cracked a smile, and even then it fades fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mmm… most of the time it’s felt very hard. I laughed once when my husband made a silly face at the baby, but it disappeared quick and I went right back to feeling flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a shower without rushing. This week, when I think about doing any of that, it feels kind of “why bother.” I still go, but the happy buzz I used to have is mostly gone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m not soothing him properly or I ate something that upset his tummy. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel it’s my fault somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke, or I’ll wake up in the night convinced the room is too cold even though the monitor says it’s fine. I know it’s probably silly, but I can’t switch the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden “can’t-catch-my-breath” feeling, like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s going on. It passes if I rock the baby or step outside, but it’s happened maybe three nights—always out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday the dishes piled up while I was trying to soothe the baby and I just stood there crying because it all felt too heavy. I manage to push through, but it’s like walking through thick mud.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—Did I fasten the swaddle tight enough? What if he spits up when I’m asleep? Most nights this week it’s taken me an hour or two to drift off, then I wake up at two or three a.m. with my heart pounding and can’t settle again for ages.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason; the sadness just sits there. Some moments are okay, but they never last long before the heaviness rolls back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve broken down a couple of times this week. Once was when I couldn’t get him to latch and I just sat there in the rocking chair with tears streaming, feeling like I’m failing at the one thing I’m supposed to be doing. Another night it hit after everyone was finally asleep and the house was quiet—everything felt hopeless and the tears came before I could stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s popped into my head once or twice, like a fleeting picture of not wanting to be here anymore, but I push it away. I’d never act on it—my baby needs me—but yeah, the thought has flickered by, especially when I feel I’m messing everything up.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood has been clouded by a constant gray heaviness: laughter comes rarely and fades quickly, activities that once excited you now feel pointless, and you often blame yourself when your baby fusses. Nearly every day brings <sym>worry</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, and a sense of drowning in ordinary tasks, while nights are spent lying awake with racing thoughts or waking with a pounding heart. Sadness, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, and fleeting images of not wanting to be here have crept in, though you're clear you would never act on them because your baby needs you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports only a single, fleeting moment of laughter amid persistent flat mood, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes loss of anticipatory joy and motivation, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ("catch myself doing that a lot") and gives specific examples of blaming herself for the baby's fussiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing anxiety "pretty much every day" with intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes classic panic attacks occurring several times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes" in frequency and severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily inability to cope, feeling overwhelmed to the point of tears and paralysis, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "Most of the time" and describes pervasive sadness that intrudes even during routine tasks.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed and hopeless, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 places you well above the EPDS threshold (≥14) indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> plus comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse core symptoms: depressed mood most of the time, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, prominent self-blame, recurrent panic-like episodes, difficulty sleeping even when exhausted, and passive suicidal ideation (Item 10 ≥1), meeting DSM-5 criteria for severity and functional impairment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>midwife</med>, or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results and create a safety plan
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full diagnostic evaluation and discussion of evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>sertraline</med>
3. Share these EPDS results and your safety thoughts with a trusted partner, family member, or friend so they can support you and help monitor warning signs
4. Consider brief daily walks, balanced meals, and five-minute breathing breaks; small structured activities can gently counter <sym>anxiety</sym> and lift mood while awaiting professional care
5. Keep crisis numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US) or your local emergency services; call immediately if thoughts of self-harm become stronger or you feel unsafe
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item self-report; responses consistent with moderate–severe symptom burden.

Dominant themes  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety (racing heart, catastrophic worries) and episodic panic (Q4, 5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and difficulty completing routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset and middle insomnia linked to intrusive worries (Q7)  
- Passive, transient self-harm ideation without intent or plan (Q10)

Risk indicators  
✓ Meets screening threshold for likely major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety  
✓ Safety concern: presence of self-harm thoughts (requires immediate safety assessment)  
✓ Functional impairment: household tasks, infant care, social withdrawal  
✓ No protective factors reported in this screen

Recommendation  
Urgent follow-up with OB/midwife or mental health provider for full diagnostic evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options.
